paper_metadata.title: Clinical heterogeneity of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: Follow-up after an interval of more than 20 years

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study uses a well-defined historical cohort with clear diagnostic criteria (ILAE 1989). The participation rate is exceptionally high (88% interviewed, 95% total inclusion via records), minimizing selection bias.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: In 1992, consecutive patients with JME at Trondheim University Hospital were identified for recruitment in a study on the association with human leukocyte antigens.
items.reasoning: The source is a hospital-based consecutive sample with baseline characteristics established in a previous study.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: In 2012, we attempted to contact all 42 patients with a request for participation in a follow-up study.
items.reasoning: The study attempted to reach the entire original cohort, reducing sampling bias.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: In 1992, consecutive patients... In 2012, we attempted to contact all 42 patients.
items.reasoning: The baseline and follow-up periods are clearly defined.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Trondheim University Hospital
items.reasoning: The specific tertiary care setting is identified.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: The clinical diagnosis of JME was based on the 1989 classification of epilepsies and epileptic syndromes by the International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE).
items.reasoning: Standardized international criteria were used for inclusion.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: 37 patients (88%) were available for a standardized semistructured telephone interview... In the remaining five, only medical records were available.
items.reasoning: A 95% inclusion rate (40/42) for the primary outcome is excellent for a 20-year follow-up.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Of the 42 patients forming the basis of this study, 25 (60%) were women. Forty patients (95%) had GTC and 12 (29%) had absences... Mean age at JME onset was 16 ± 3.2 years.
items.reasoning: Key demographics and clinical seizure characteristics are provided.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Attrition is minimal. Only 2 patients were completely lost to follow-up (no fixed address), and the status of deceased patients was accounted for using medical records.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: In 40 patients seizure outcome was known at least 20 years after JME onset.
items.reasoning: 40 out of 42 patients (95%) is a very high retention rate for a long-term study.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Two other deceased patients followed for more than 20 years were included based on their medical records. Two patients could not be contacted as they were currently registered with no fixed address; in one medical records were sufficient for inclusion.
items.reasoning: The authors explicitly describe using medical records to supplement missing interview data.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: One patient could not be included as he died after only 13 years of follow-up... Two patients could not be contacted as they were currently registered with no fixed address.
items.reasoning: Specific reasons (death before 20 years, lack of address) are provided.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: While reasons for loss are given, a detailed comparison of baseline characteristics between the 2 lost patients and the 40 included patients is not explicitly tabulated.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Beyond that, we found no association between drop-out from follow-up and social outcome.
items.reasoning: The authors state they checked for associations with drop-out, though the sample size of drop-outs is too small for robust statistical comparison.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Prognostic factors (seizure types and timing) were collected retrospectively via medical records and patient recall during interviews, which introduces potential recall bias for events occurring decades ago.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: MC habitually or occasionally preceding GTC (clonic–tonic–clonic seizure)... delay of more than one year between MC onset and first GTC.
items.reasoning: The prognostic factors (seizure patterns) are clearly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: 37 patients (88%) were available for a standardized semistructured telephone interview... Medical records were reviewed for background information.
items.reasoning: While medical records were used, much of the clinical history relies on patient recall over a 20-year span, which is subject to bias.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: >1 year between onset of myoclonic seizures and GTC
items.reasoning: The 1-year cut-off is a standard clinical milestone in epilepsy history.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: 37 patients (88%) were available for a standardized semistructured telephone interview.
items.reasoning: A standardized interview protocol was used for the majority of the cohort.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: In 40 patients seizure outcome was known
items.reasoning: Data was available for nearly the entire cohort.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: Imputation is not mentioned; however, missing data was minimal.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The primary outcome (seizure remission) is self-reported via telephone interview. While this is standard for long-term epilepsy follow-up, it lacks objective verification (e.g., EEG or diary) and is subject to recall bias.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: 21 were in remission for >5 years. Seven were off antiepileptic drugs (AEDs), four being seizure free for >10 years.
items.reasoning: Remission is clearly defined by duration (5 and 10 years).

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: standardized semistructured telephone interview, focusing on seizure types, seizure frequency, medication and psychosocial outcome.
items.reasoning: Telephone interviews are common but less reliable than prospective diaries or witnessed accounts.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: 37 agreed to a semi-structured interview. In the remaining five, only medical records were available.
items.reasoning: The majority were interviewed, but a small subset relied solely on record review, which is a different measurement setting.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study primarily reports univariable associations (Chi-square/t-tests). There is no multivariable adjustment for potential confounders like AED type, dosage, or psychiatric comorbidity when assessing the relationship between PFs and seizure outcome.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: focusing on seizure types, seizure frequency, medication and psychosocial outcome... psychiatric comorbidity, seven with substance or alcohol abuse.
items.reasoning: The authors measured medication use and psychiatric status, which are key confounders.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: Psychosocial outcome was assessed based on five elements: graduation from high school, disability or unemployment benefits, alcohol or illegal substance abuse...
items.reasoning: Psychosocial factors are defined, but medication 'dose' and 'duration' are not detailed for all participants.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Social network, as well as perceived satisfaction with health, was simply graded as poor, sufficient or good
items.reasoning: Subjective grading by the patient is less reliable than validated psychiatric scales.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: 37 patients (88%) were available for a standardized semistructured telephone interview
items.reasoning: The interview process was standardized for the main cohort.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: No mention of handling missing confounder data.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: Chi-square test and independent t-test were used for comparison of categorical and continuous variables, respectively.
items.reasoning: The study design did not involve matching or stratification to control for confounding.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: p < 0.05 was considered significant.
items.reasoning: Only univariable analyses were performed; no multivariable regression was used to adjust for confounders.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The analysis is simple and transparent, but the lack of multivariable modeling limits the validity of the prognostic claims. The small sample size (n=40) likely precluded complex modeling.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: Chi-square test and independent t-test were used for comparison of categorical and continuous variables, respectively.
items.reasoning: The strategy is simple and clearly stated.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: There was no multivariable model building described.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: Chi-square test and independent t-test
items.reasoning: While appropriate for simple comparisons, these tests do not allow for the prognostic modeling usually expected in QUIPS (e.g., Cox regression).

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: The relationship between various clinical characteristics and five-year seizure remission is shown in Table 3.
items.reasoning: The authors report both significant and non-significant findings (e.g., p=0.069, p=0.464).
